title: Fields white for harvest (John 4:27–42)
hookLine: she leaves her water jar and tells the town; many believe

lines: THE DISCIPLES COME BACK WITH LUNCH.
THE JAR STAYS BY THE WELL.
cards: Just as Jesus tells her who he is, the disciples come back with lunch. John says they marveled that he was talking with a woman, and nobody dared ask him why. A group of men holding bread, standing awkwardly.

The woman doesn't wait for anyone to explain. She walks fast back toward town, and she leaves the one thing she came for sitting by the well. "The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city."

teach.b: Why mention the jar? It was the whole reason for her trip. Leaving it says she's in a hurry, and maybe that she'll be back.
Some readers hear more: she came for ordinary water and found living water, so the old jar can wait.
In town, her message is simple, almost funny: "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" Not a sermon.
An invitation, and a question, close to the one Jesus first asked back in chapter one: what seek ye?
Meanwhile, the disciples are pushing food at Jesus. Master, eat. He says, "I have meat to eat that ye know not of."
Meat, in King James English, just means food. They wonder if someone brought him something. His food, he explains, is to do the will of the one who sent him.

Then he points at the fields: "Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest."

Some readers picture the townspeople at that moment, streaming across the fields toward the well, maybe in light-colored clothes. The text doesn't say so, but the timing fits. Many Samaritans believe because of her word.
Then Jesus stays two days, more believe, and they tell her: "Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves."
She brought them; they met him themselves. And they call him the Savior of the world.

how: Some Christians turn to this passage when they talk about sharing their faith, hearing in the woman's "come, see" a model of inviting someone rather than arguing.

games.q: you're the woman. you've just heard the stranger say who he is, and his friends are staring at you. what do you do?
o: fill your jar quietly and go home.
leave the jar and run to tell the town.
wait for the disciples to explain.
games.why: she leaves her waterpot and goes into the city: "come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did."

practice: Think of something good that happened to you lately, a kindness, a book, a moment that opened something, and picture the face of someone who'd want to hear about it.
Then name your water jar, the small thing that usually stops you sharing, being busy or worrying it'll sound strange, and let it sit by the well a while.
If you pray, ask for the nerve to say come and see; if not, just rest with the person you pictured.

wordCard.voice: Harvest. Jesus's words as the Samaritan town comes out to meet him: the harvest isn't months away, it's already here.

orig.note: Greek: white, bright. The fields are already pale, ready to cut.
